extracted.intended_audience: general readers, travellers, students and practitioners of architecture and art history interested in Venetian Byzantine architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and evaluative description of Byzantine palaces in Venice, focusing on proportions, arcade arrangement, capitals, ornamentation, and the aesthetic principles that determine beauty and authenticity. Aimed at identifying the formal features and subtleties that characterize Byzantine workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of antiquity from fragments and fabric
rubrics_metrics.description: The impossibility of finding so much as an angle or a single story in perfect condition is a proof... that they were indeed raised during the earliest phases of the Venetian power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dispersed fragments (a capital, a segment of an arch, foundation blocks) and their architectural method as proof of original antiquity; if minute correspondences of arrangement are traceable in fragments, they indicate original positions. Anti-pattern: assuming age or originality from later restorations or modernized ground floors without correlating fragmentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central-and-wings arcade composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Arcades divided into a centre and wings; centre indicated by greater size in the midmost arches and by alternation of shafts in the centre with pilasters or small shafts at the flanks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate façades by checking continuous arcades across fronts, the presence of a central group larger than flanking groups, and alternation of full shafts and pilasters. Example: Fondaco de' Turchi and Casa Loredan. Anti-pattern: treating a uniform arcade as Byzantine without these central-wing distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-tier arching pattern (lower tall/few, upper shorter/many)
rubrics_metrics.description: They agree also in having tall and few arches in their lower stories, and shorter and more numerous arches above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify Byzantine composition by at least two tiers of arches with this vertical differentiation. Note that modern alterations often destroy one tier; if one tier is modernized, evaluate remaining tier for original characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle gradation and cadence of arch widths
rubrics_metrics.description: Gradual cadence to the flanks, from eight feet down to four and a half, in a series of continually increasing steps; differences of inches (even two inches) were used to satisfy the builder's eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess beauty and authenticity by measuring incremental changes across arch spans—minute differences are intentional. Examples: varied reductions between adjacent arches in Fondaco de' Turchi, Casa Loredan, Casa Farsetti. Anti-pattern: dismissing small discrepancies as errors or noise; they may be deliberate harmonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shafts as echoes and dovetailing devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The way in which the large shaft is used as an echo of those in the central arcade, dovetailing them into the system of pilasters, is highly characteristic of the Byzantine care in composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the relationship between central and flank arcades by how large shafts are positioned to 'echo' central elements and mediate to pilasters—this dovetailing indicates considered composition rather than ad hoc additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minute harmonies of proportion indicate single school/original form
rubrics_metrics.description: These singular and minute harmonies of proportion indicate, beyond all dispute, not only that the buildings in which they are found are of one school, but... in their original form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurring, subtle proportional coincidences across buildings to argue for a common workmanship/school and original arrangement. Anti-pattern: attributing repeated subtle proportions to chance or later imitation without measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor arches/porticos as proportional devices (ornamental rather than functional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two minor arches at the extremities... are of no use whatever except to consummate the proportions of the façade, and themselves to exhibit the most exquisite proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some architectural elements exist primarily for proportioning the façade; evaluate facades not only for function but for proportional augmentation. Anti-pattern: assuming every architectural projection must serve a practical function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal families of capitals: convex and concave
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two great orders of capitals in the world; one is convex in its contour, the other concave; richness of ornament with all freedom of fancy is for the most part found in the one, and severity of ornament with stern discipline of the fancy in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify capitals into convex (broad, cushion-like, often richer) and concave (longer-lived, extends into Gothic) families. Use family characteristics to date, locate, and understand functional choice (e.g., Corinthian-like forms reserved for nave pillars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitals modeled on natural flower-types for distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Both families may be generally represented by considering them formed upon the types of flowers — the one upon that of the water-lily (convex), the other upon that of the convolvulus (concave).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison with natural flower outlines to identify and fix capital types; this natural analogy helps distinguish profiles and varieties of capitals in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of capital types by building program
rubrics_metrics.description: The pure Corinthian form should have been reserved almost exclusively for nave pillars... it occurs together with almost every other form on the exterior of St. Mark's, but never so definitely as in the nave and transept shafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate placement of more elaborate Corinthian or large concave capitals (nave) versus simpler small-shaft capitals (palaces/flanks) to infer function and relative importance of spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life in ornamentation: variation, naturalism, asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only is every one of these capitals differently fancied, but there are many of them which have no two sides alike... the leaves are, every one of them, more founded on realities, sketched... from the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ornament vitality by looking for varied motifs on different sides, naturalistic leaf treatment, and deliberate asymmetries (birds, grapes, vine-leaves varied). Anti-pattern: rigid, purely symmetrical repetition indicates less 'life' and an older or more academic approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and grand curves subordinating detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The excessive breadth of the masses... grand and simple curves... subdues all their multitudinous points and foldings to its own inevitable dominion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value unity produced by broad, enclosing curves that govern minute detailing—look for large-scale forms that unify and direct the eye. Anti-pattern: overly fussy detail without an enclosing mass or curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle generalization and enclosure of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The sculptor... could not rest until he had enclosed [leaves] with an unbroken line, like that of a pointed arch... the feeling which bound his prickly leaves... into those broad masses of unbroken flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and prefer compositions where detailed elements are subordinated by an enclosing, unifying outline or motif—this indicates a mature aesthetic sensibility akin to later Renaissance unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurements and minute numerical differences matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If he will only take the little pains necessary to compare them, he will, I am almost certain, find the result not devoid of interest... the eye is continually influenced by what it cannot detect; nay, it is not going too far to say, that it is most influenced by what it detects least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful measurement of spans, intervals, and heights; accept that very small differences (inches) were deliberate and contribute to aesthetic effect. Anti-pattern: dismissing small metric irregularities as irrelevant to beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic profiling and construction of Byzantine capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: The convex family is modelled upon rounded cups... the concave group bends below into the convex bell-shape... capitals often obtained from a square block by cutting off corners and rounding edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify Byzantine capitals by their constructional profiles (rounded bells, bulging concave to convex transitions, abacuses, fillets) and by common carving methods and surface treatments; use profiles to distinguish pure concave, pure convex, and transitional types.

rubrics_metrics.name: External form reveals internal disposition (central loggia and light)
rubrics_metrics.description: They indicate to us a form... in which there were, universally, central galleries, or loggias, opening into apartments on each wing, the amount of light admitted being immense; and the general proportions of the building, slender, light, and graceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer internal arrangements (e.g., central galleries admitting light) from the external arcade and shaft composition—external proportions (slender aggregate of shafts and arches) suggest internal light and plan. Anti-pattern: assuming interior layout without correlating to external arcade evidence.
